Build a polished, fully offline-first iOS voice-journaling app called
"Fieldnotes". Native Apple stack only: SwiftUI + SwiftData, AVFoundation
for recording, Speech framework for on-device transcription, Natural­
Language framework for on-device tagging/sentiment, PencilKit for sketch
annotations. No backend, no accounts, no network dependency for any core
feature — everything must work in airplane mode. Follow the
ios-app-factory-rules. If a requested capability needs something this
project genuinely cannot provide (a special Apple entitlement, a paid
developer account feature, server-side ML), do NOT fake or stub it —
record it as an explicit gap with what it would actually take.

Core features (complete over broad — ship fewer things fully working):

1. Voice entries: record audio journal entries with a live waveform
   view while recording. Recording must survive being interrupted by a
   phone call, Siri, or the app being backgrounded, and must resume
   or cleanly finalize the entry rather than corrupt/lose it — get
   AVAudioSession category/interruption handling genuinely right, this
   is the hardest technical part of the app.
2. On-device transcription: transcribe each recording using Speech
   framework (on-device recognition only — reject/flag if only
   server-based recognition is available for a locale). Transcript is
   editable after the fact; edits must not desync from the audio
   timeline (tapping a transcript sentence seeks the audio to that
   point).
3. Auto-tagging & mood: run NaturalLanguage tokenization/sentiment on
   each transcript to suggest tags and a mood score. Suggestions are
   editable/dismissible — never silently apply an AI guess as fact.
4. Sketch annotations: attach PencilKit sketches to any entry (finger
   or Pencil), stored alongside the audio/transcript.
5. Bi-directional linking: entries can @-mention/link other entries;
   each entry shows a "linked from" backlinks section computed live
   from the local store (no manual backlink maintenance) — same
   integrity discipline as a graph/notes app: linking, unlinking, and
   deleting an entry must never leave a dangling or duplicate backlink.
6. Search: full-text search across transcripts AND tags/mood, with
   results ranked by a real relevance score you define and document
   (not just substring match order).
7. HealthKit correlation (read-only, explicit permission): show each
   entry's mood alongside that day's HealthKit sleep/activity summary
   if authorized, and degrade to "not connected" honestly if denied —
   never block core journaling on this permission.
8. Home-screen widget + Live Activity: widget shows the latest entry's
   mood/snippet; a Live Activity shows elapsed time and live waveform
   while actively recording, ending cleanly when the recording stops
   or the app is killed mid-recording (no orphaned Live Activity).
9. Share Extension (separate target): accept shared text or a photo
   from other apps and create a new Fieldnotes entry from it.
10. App Intents: "Start a voice entry" and "Search my journal" exposed
    to Shortcuts/Siri.
11. CarPlay: a minimal CarPlay scene for hands-free start/stop
    recording while driving. This requires Apple's CarPlay audio-app
    entitlement, which a personal free developer account cannot
    obtain — if that's confirmed true in this environment, build the
    CarPlay scene code path correctly but record in Gaps that it
    cannot actually run/ship without that entitlement, rather than
    silently omitting the feature or pretending it works.

Priorities, in order: (a) audio-session interruption correctness — a
lost or corrupted recording is the worst possible failure, (b) backlink
graph integrity, (c) honest degradation of every permission-gated
feature (Speech, HealthKit, CarPlay). Use Decimal/Int for anything
numeric that isn't inherently floating (durations in seconds as
TimeInterval is fine; don't invent unnecessary Decimal use here — this
app's money-precision lesson from prior apps doesn't apply, there's no
currency). Seed a "demo entries" toggle in Settings with realistic
sample entries, transcripts, tags, and backlinks so no screen is empty
on first review. Provide a clear way to run it in the iOS Simulator via
Xcode, and call out anywhere CarPlay/HealthKit/Speech behave differently
in Simulator vs. a real device.

Now my actual read on this, wearing the "what quietly breaks" hat.

The single biggest risk to this whole build is that priority (a) — audio-session interruption correctness — is exactly the kind of requirement that's easy to claim is done and hard to actually prove is done. AVAudioSession interruption handling (begin/end interruption notifications, `.shouldResume` option, route changes from AirPods disconnect, Siri duck-and-resume, a phone call arriving, the app going to background then getting killed by the system for memory pressure) has a huge number of edge cases, and the iOS Simulator cannot simulate a real phone call or a real Bluetooth route change. Any later phase that says "tested interruption handling" needs to specify exactly what was tested (which notifications, which transition simulated how) because "handled interruptions" without a concrete test method is an unverifiable claim, not a fact. I want a decision rule that no phase gets to mark this requirement done without naming the specific interruption scenarios exercised and how (real device required for phone-call and Bluetooth-route scenarios; background-kill can be approximated via Xcode's "Simulate Memory Warning" / debugger detach but that's an approximation, not proof).

Second risk: several of these features have hidden cross-cutting dependencies the prompt doesn't spell out but that will break integrity if skipped. The widget and Live Activity need to read the same SwiftData store as the main app, which means an App Group container and a shared model container — if that's not set up, the widget will either crash, show stale/no data, or the build will silently fall back to fake placeholder data (which the global rules explicitly forbid: "No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data"). Same for the Share Extension — it needs an App Group to write into the same store the main app reads, or shared entries silently vanish. This should be a hard requirement even though the user didn't say the words "App Group."

Third: "ending cleanly when the app is killed mid-recording (no orphaned Live Activity)" is a very strong guarantee. iOS does not reliably run app code at the moment of a force-kill — there's no guaranteed clean-shutdown hook. The realistic mechanism is: request the Live Activity with a sensible stale/timeout date up front, and reconcile/end any stale activity on next launch — not "detect the kill and clean up live." If the team quietly implements only the happy-path stop-button flow and calls the kill-scenario "handled," that's a false claim. I want the contract to state the actual mechanism (staleDate + relaunch reconciliation) as the definition of "clean" here, so nobody promises something iOS can't do.

Fourth, on honesty about gaps: the prompt pre-empts one gap (CarPlay entitlement) but there are at least two more real candidates that deserve the same treatment rather than being discovered late: (1) HealthKit — reading HealthKit data for real requires the HealthKit capability/entitlement in the provisioning profile, which is available on a free personal-team account for local device testing but not for TestFlight/App Store distribution without a paid account; that distinction should be recorded explicitly, not asserted as either "fully works" or "fully blocked." (2) On-device Speech recognition support is locale- and device-dependent (`SFSpeechRecognizer.supportsOnDeviceRecognition`, and it can be `false` even when the framework itself is available) — the contract needs a decision rule for what "reject/flag" actually means in the running app: does the record button get disabled, does the user see an explicit banner, does the entry still get created with transcription marked as unavailable? That has to be decided now, not improvised later, because "flag" is not a UI behavior.

Fifth, the "real relevance score you define and document" requirement is a trap for hand-waving — it's trivial to ship a search that's actually just weighted substring matching while calling it a relevance score. The contract should require the scoring formula (whatever it is — recency-weighted BM25-lite, field-weighted term frequency, whatever's chosen) to be written down as a concrete, checkable spec, and the testable requirement should be "given two entries where one has more matching terms in transcript vs one has a matching tag, verify the ranking matches the documented formula's prediction," not just "search returns results."

Sixth, backlink integrity: the prompt's bar ("no dangling or duplicate backlink" on link/unlink/delete) needs a precise definition of what "delete" does to inbound links — does deleting entry A remove the backlink pointer from B, or does B's link to A become a dead/broken-link chip that's shown as such? Both are legitimate designs but they have to be picked explicitly, because "no dangling backlink" and "show broken link honestly" can conflict if not specified.

**Codex (Design Lead · Skeptic) — Round 1**

This points to a privacy-first, interruption-prone journaling workflow, not a broad productivity app. The strongest audience is people who want one-gesture capture during life noise (walking, commuting, driving prep, post-meeting decompression), and who want text/searchable recall later without trusting cloud sync. The highest-value user gain is “start recording fast, survive reality, recall accurately,” where reality means calls, Siri interruptions, backgrounding, and imperfect speech availability (ASSUMPTION based on typical real-world usage patterns).

For a competitive map, the key pattern set I’d borrow from is: Apple Voice Memos for low-friction capture flow, Apple Health for trusted local health summaries, and Obsidian/Notion/Day One style linking and timeline thinking. Apple Voice Memos does recording/organization well but is weak at structured long-form semantic retrieval across linked entries, and its notebook-like graph story is thin (ASSUMPTION). Day One has polished journaling and media attachment UX but typically relies more on cloud sync patterns and less strict offline-first guarantees (ASSUMPTION). Obsidian has strong bi-directional links and backlink discoverability but is not a native, always-on voice-first mobile journaling default and has friction around quick capture in iOS-native gesture flow (ASSUMPTION). The Fieldnotes gap is clear: native SwiftUI-first local journaling that combines interruption-safe voice capture + transcript timing integrity + sketch + backlinks + search ranking in one no-network, no-account experience.

On iOS specifically, the native opportunities are unusually strong: AVFoundation for stable audio lifecycle, Speech on-device checks for locale-aware behavior, NaturalLanguage for local tag/mood suggestions, SwiftData for a fast typed local graph model, and App Group shared storage to keep app, widget, intents, and share extension in one source of truth (critical, and already contract-bound). ActivityKit + WidgetKit can make recording state visible without reopening the app, which is not just polish but trust: users can verify that recordings are running and ending behavior is consistent. PencilKit makes “field note + quick sketch” feel native for both stylus and finger inputs. App Intents + Siri can turn this into a hands-off tool, but those surfaces must not be the emotional center of the first build.

The biggest risk in my own direction is that this can quietly become a “feature theater” app where every target exists superficially except the recorder integrity and link integrity promises. The design should treat “interruption-safe recording” and “tamper-proof link graph” as design pillars, not engineering details; otherwise the product feels premium but fails at the moments that matter.

For assumptions, I’m calling out the key ones explicitly: users prefer local-only storage over cloud sync even if that means slower cross-device portability (ASSUMPTION); on-device speech availability will be a real limiter in some locales and users will accept a clear “not available” state if clearly framed (ASSUMPTION); and people will value stable timeline anchors over perfect automatic transcript quality (ASSUMPTION). Unknowns to stress-test now: whether Siri/phone-call interruption paths stay robust across real devices without app restart logic corner cases (ASSUMPTION), whether users can tolerate the explicit degraded state when transcription is unavailable (ASSUMPTION), and whether widget/live activity state should prioritize honesty over continuity UX during force-kill windows (contract-bound, resolved with residual-window caveat).

For the first build, the UX should narrow to: 1) one main recorder flow with explicit live-state indicators and immutable interruption states, 2) one entry detail screen with audio, editable transcript anchored by ID, tags/mood suggestions as dismissible UI, sketch attachment, and visible broken-link handling, 3) backlinks surface computed from live store state, 4) search screen that always explains why matches exist even without transcripts, and 5) settings-driven demo data seeding to ensure onboarding reviewability without data contamination. I would defer feature chrome not required for trust (analytics, advanced mood storytelling, deep widget variants) and ship first a reliable, inspectable core.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Pragmatist) — Round 1**

Reading this as a QA/pragmatist, not a visionary: I want to know what actually breaks first, and what's the smallest thing we can ship that's genuinely trustworthy rather than merely feature-complete.

On audience — this reads as a single-user, privacy-first personal journal for people who've been burned by (or are suspicious of) cloud journaling and voice-note tools. Likely overlap with two groups: people already using Day One or Daylio for reflective/mood journaling, and people who like the Obsidian/Roam bidirectional-linking mental model and want that applied to voice rather than typed notes (ASSUMPTION — no market data was fetched for this project, this is inference from the feature list, not research). Use context is probably solo, end-of-day or in-the-moment reflection, sometimes in-car (hence CarPlay), sometimes processing something emotionally loaded — which raises the stakes on "never fake completion state" higher than a typical notes app, because losing or corrupting a recording of someone's actual therapy-processing session is a worse trust violation than losing a to-do note.

On comparables: Day One is the incumbent to beat on polish and has audio/photo entries, but it's fundamentally cloud-sync-centric and doesn't do transcript-to-audio-timeline seeking or a computed backlink graph (ASSUMPTION, based on general familiarity with the product, not a fetched source). Apple's own Voice Memos app already does on-device transcription in recent iOS versions (ASSUMPTION/general knowledge) — which matters a lot for how this app should be pitched, because "we transcribe on-device" alone is no longer a differentiator, Apple ships that natively now. The actual differentiator in this feature list is the combination: transcript+audio+tags+mood+backlinks+HealthKit context in one graph-aware local store. Obsidian/Roam prove the backlink UX pattern works and that users tolerate "computed live" backlinks over manual link management, which validates DEC-prompt_contract-008's approach. None of these comparables combine voice-first capture with a linking graph, so that's the real gap — but it's also why this is the hardest possible v1 to build well, since it's assembling patterns from three different app categories (journaling, transcription, graph notes) that don't normally coexist.

Here's my actual worry, wearing the pragmatist hat: eleven features plus a widget plus a Live Activity plus a Share Extension plus App Intents plus a CarPlay scene is not "a first build," it's a portfolio of five apps stitched together. The prompt contract already got the priority order right (interruption correctness > backlinks > honest degradation), but product research should say the quiet part out loud: a genuinely shippable v1 is the core loop — record, interruption-safe, transcribe, tag/mood suggest, backlink, search — done to the "20+ scenario-tested" bar the contract demands. Widget and Live Activity are next because they're actually testable in Simulator and reuse the same App Group work. Share Extension and App Intents are real but secondary surfaces. CarPlay gets code-path-only treatment with zero polish time, per the contract's own instruction.

Concrete risks I'd flag before anyone starts building:

First, there's a nasty inversion in this project: the single most safety-critical requirement (interruption correctness under a real phone call, Bluetooth route change, force-quit) is the *least* verifiable in the environment this will actually be reviewed in. Whoever reviews this build will almost certainly do it in Simulator first, where you cannot place a real call or trigger a real Bluetooth handoff. That means the flagship trust guarantee is the one most likely to get a superficial "looks fine" pass unless the build phase is explicit that Simulator-passing is not the same as scenario-verified, exactly per DEC-prompt_contract-002.

Second, CarPlay's gate may be tighter than "needs a paid account" implies. My understanding (ASSUMPTION/general knowledge, not fetched) is that the CarPlay audio-app entitlement historically requires a specific request/approval from Apple even for local development and testing via Xcode's CarPlay simulator scene, not just a paid Apple Developer Program membership — a paid account is necessary but may not be sufficient. That should get confirmed as fact rather than repeating the assumption that a paid account alone unlocks it; if wrong, the gap note overpromises what upgrading the account would fix.

Third, HealthKit correlation's "connected" state is probably not the common case in review conditions. Nobody reviewing this app will have real sleep/activity history matched to demo journal entries unless it's hand-seeded into the Simulator's Health app for that exact purpose. That means the "not connected / denied" honest-degradation path is what most reviewers will actually see day-to-day, and it should be built and polished as the primary state, not the fallback branch — the connected state is the one that needs the seeded-data workaround to even demo.

Fourth, the App Group + shared SwiftData container isn't just plumbing, it's real integration risk: the widget's timeline provider, the Live Activity, the Share Extension, and the main app all touching one shared local store concurrently is exactly the kind of surface where schema mismatches or write contention produce silent staleness — which would look like "the widget shows an old entry" and get misdiagnosed as a caching bug rather than what it actually is, a shared-store consistency bug.

Fifth, sentiment from NaturalLanguage is coarse — positive/negative/neutral polarity, not a clinically meaningful mood measure — and the UI needs to set that expectation plainly (a small score/label, framed as a rough signal) rather than imply the app understands the user's emotional state, both because it'd be dishonest and because overclaiming here is the kind of thing that erodes trust fast in a journaling app specifically.

For the first build, my implication is: bias every hour of build time toward the five core-loop requirements and the App Group foundation under them, since that foundation is what widget/Live Activity/Share Extension/App Intents all depend on later — get that shared-store plumbing right once rather than retrofitting it after the widget already exists. Treat HealthKit's denied/not-connected state as the default design case. Treat CarPlay purely as a compiling code path with an accurate, specific Gap note once its entitlement requirements are actually confirmed rather than assumed. And build the demo-entries seed data to include a HealthKit-correlated day and a broken-link example specifically, since those are the two states most likely to otherwise go unseen in a normal review pass.

- NaturalLanguage sentiment is coarse polarity, not clinical mood — overclaiming this would erode trust in a journaling app specifically.

**Implications for the first build:** Scope the true v1 to the core loop (record → interruption-safe finalize/resume → on-device transcribe → tag/mood suggestions → live backlinks → documented-relevance search), built on top of the App Group + shared SwiftData container as foundational work done once. Global app-build rules:
- Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
- Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
- For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
- Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
- No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.
- The interface must never claim an outcome that has not happened: show Saved/Deleted/Sent/Synced/Unlocked only after it is truly confirmed, never a success state shown unconditionally. No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data.
- Implement the design spec's tokens as one SwiftUI theme file (e.g. Theme.swift with type, spacing, and color definitions) and reference it everywhere; never scatter font/size/color literals through views.
- Every generated app must fully support dark mode: semantic color roles with explicit light and dark values, verified in both appearances.

Now my actual read on this, wearing the "what quietly breaks" hat.

The single biggest risk to this whole build is that priority (a) — audio-session interruption correctness — is exactly the kind of requirement that's easy to claim is done and hard to actually prove is done. AVAudioSession interruption handling (begin/end interruption notifications, `.shouldResume` option, route changes from AirPods disconnect, Siri duck-and-resume, a phone call arriving, the app going to background then getting killed by the system for memory pressure) has a huge number of edge cases, and the iOS Simulator cannot simulate a real phone call or a real Bluetooth route change. Any later phase that says "tested interruption handling" needs to specify exactly what was tested (which notifications, which transition simulated how) because "handled interruptions" without a concrete test method is an unverifiable claim, not a fact. I want a decision rule that no phase gets to mark this requirement done without naming the specific interruption scenarios exercised and how (real device required for phone-call and Bluetooth-route scenarios; background-kill can be approximated via Xcode's "Simulate Memory Warning" / debugger detach but that's an approximation, not proof).

Second risk: several of these features have hidden cross-cutting dependencies the prompt doesn't spell out but that will break integrity if skipped. The widget and Live Activity need to read the same SwiftData store as the main app, which means an App Group container and a shared model container — if that's not set up, the widget will either crash, show stale/no data, or the build will silently fall back to fake placeholder data (which the global rules explicitly forbid: "No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data"). Same for the Share Extension — it needs an App Group to write into the same store the main app reads, or shared entries silently vanish. This should be a hard requirement even though the user didn't say the words "App Group."

Third: "ending cleanly when the app is killed mid-recording (no orphaned Live Activity)" is a very strong guarantee. iOS does not reliably run app code at the moment of a force-kill — there's no guaranteed clean-shutdown hook. The realistic mechanism is: request the Live Activity with a sensible stale/timeout date up front, and reconcile/end any stale activity on next launch — not "detect the kill and clean up live." If the team quietly implements only the happy-path stop-button flow and calls the kill-scenario "handled," that's a false claim. I want the contract to state the actual mechanism (staleDate + relaunch reconciliation) as the definition of "clean" here, so nobody promises something iOS can't do.

Fourth, on honesty about gaps: the prompt pre-empts one gap (CarPlay entitlement) but there are at least two more real candidates that deserve the same treatment rather than being discovered late: (1) HealthKit — reading HealthKit data for real requires the HealthKit capability/entitlement in the provisioning profile, which is available on a free personal-team account for local device testing but not for TestFlight/App Store distribution without a paid account; that distinction should be recorded explicitly, not asserted as either "fully works" or "fully blocked." (2) On-device Speech recognition support is locale- and device-dependent (`SFSpeechRecognizer.supportsOnDeviceRecognition`, and it can be `false` even when the framework itself is available) — the contract needs a decision rule for what "reject/flag" actually means in the running app: does the record button get disabled, does the user see an explicit banner, does the entry still get created with transcription marked as unavailable? That has to be decided now, not improvised later, because "flag" is not a UI behavior.

Fifth, the "real relevance score you define and document" requirement is a trap for hand-waving — it's trivial to ship a search that's actually just weighted substring matching while calling it a relevance score. The contract should require the scoring formula (whatever it is — recency-weighted BM25-lite, field-weighted term frequency, whatever's chosen) to be written down as a concrete, checkable spec, and the testable requirement should be "given two entries where one has more matching terms in transcript vs one has a matching tag, verify the ranking matches the documented formula's prediction," not just "search returns results."

Sixth, backlink integrity: the prompt's bar ("no dangling or duplicate backlink" on link/unlink/delete) needs a precise definition of what "delete" does to inbound links — does deleting entry A remove the backlink pointer from B, or does B's link to A become a dead/broken-link chip that's shown as such? Both are legitimate designs but they have to be picked explicitly, because "no dangling backlink" and "show broken link honestly" can conflict if not specified.

This points to a privacy-first, interruption-prone journaling workflow, not a broad productivity app. The strongest audience is people who want one-gesture capture during life noise (walking, commuting, driving prep, post-meeting decompression), and who want text/searchable recall later without trusting cloud sync. The highest-value user gain is “start recording fast, survive reality, recall accurately,” where reality means calls, Siri interruptions, backgrounding, and imperfect speech availability (ASSUMPTION based on typical real-world usage patterns).

For a competitive map, the key pattern set I’d borrow from is: Apple Voice Memos for low-friction capture flow, Apple Health for trusted local health summaries, and Obsidian/Notion/Day One style linking and timeline thinking. Apple Voice Memos does recording/organization well but is weak at structured long-form semantic retrieval across linked entries, and its notebook-like graph story is thin (ASSUMPTION). Day One has polished journaling and media attachment UX but typically relies more on cloud sync patterns and less strict offline-first guarantees (ASSUMPTION). Obsidian has strong bi-directional links and backlink discoverability but is not a native, always-on voice-first mobile journaling default and has friction around quick capture in iOS-native gesture flow (ASSUMPTION). The Fieldnotes gap is clear: native SwiftUI-first local journaling that combines interruption-safe voice capture + transcript timing integrity + sketch + backlinks + search ranking in one no-network, no-account experience.

    case .userCancelled, .pending:

func checkVerified<T>(_ result: VerificationResult<T>) throws -> T {
    switch result {
    case .unverified(_, let error): throw error   // signature failed — do NOT grant

}
